paper_title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user-centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neurons, each encoding multiple unrelated concepts, hinder localizing the components behind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personalize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized latents, from which we identify the experts encoding distinct personalization features. The personalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters, exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal interventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model's behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, revealing distinct routing paths for different personalization features.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) adapts LLMs to user or group preferences (Salemi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b). Due to increasing demand for AI-assisted user-centric applications, Personalization of LLMs has become an important research direction. Most methods use dense LLMs (Zhang et al., 2025b), offering little interpretability 1Code and data: persona_moe_explain https://github.com/copenlu/ 1 of localizing important model components encoding distinct personalized features due to the polysemanticity of encoding multiple orthogonal concepts into single neuron (Olah et al., 2020). Recent work on developing intrinsically interpretable LLMs suggests that wider, more sparse LLMs enable their neurons to capture more disentangled features and reduce polysemanticity (Yang et al., 2025b). Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs offer scalable solution for wider and sparser networks by replacing dense FFN block in the MLP layer with set of experts of the same size, using sparse routing mechanism to select subset of these experts to process each input token (Shazeer et al., 2017). This mechanism enables MoE LLMs to offer better interpretability for downstream tasks by achieving lower polysemanticity (Herbst et al., 2026), where experts encode distinct task-specific features. Motivated by these observations, we utilize MoE LLMs for personalization and subsequent interpretability analysis, addressing research questions covering polysemamticity of MoE LLMs for personalization (RQ1, 6.2), identifying distinct personalized features encoded via experts during personalization (RQ2, 6.3), and localizing unique routing paths for distinct personalized features (RQ3, 6.4). Following Bai et al. (2025) on MoE LLMs alignment, we adapt the MoE LLMs towards personalization using two-stage parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) (4.1), on large-scale personalization dataset covering diverse preferences for user groups, MULTIFACETED COLLECTION (Lee et al., 2024). We then train sparse autoencoderbased (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024) architecture crosscoder (Minder et al., 2025) on paired personalized and non-personalized activations to identify interpretable personalization latents. Mapping these latents to experts reveals distinct routing paths associated with personalization. Our proposed method is illustrated in Figure 1. Extensive experiments on three open-weight Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework: [Bottom Top] For given query and user preference via system message, we collect activations for all tokens of the input prompt from particular layer of personalized (Left) and non-personalized (Right) MoE and then train SAE-based model (crosscoder) to learn and identify set of latents associated with the personalized MoE LLMs capturing distinct personalization features. instruction-tuned decoder-only MoE LLMs, OLMoE-1B-7B (0125), Qwen3-30B-A3B (2507), and Mixtral-8x7B (v0.1), spanning three personalization benchmarks: MULTIFACETED BENCH (Lee et al., 2024) covering preferences for user groups, and LaMP and LongLaMP benchmarks for per user preference, verifies the scalability of MoE LLMs in personalization by outperforming similar active parameter sized dense LLMs and achieve competitive performance against similar total parameter sized dense LLMs, while utilizing only 20% of the total parameters per token (6.1). Furthermore, MoE LLMs enable better learning of crosscoder to identify high-quality small set of latents (less than 0.25% of total latents), highly contributing in explaining distinct personalized features encoded during personalization than dense LLMs, verifying lower polysemanticity for personalization (6.2). These personalized latents each capture distinct personalization feature (6.3) and map onto small, stable set of specialized experts (6.4), revealing distinct routing paths for personalization in MoE LLMs. Causal interventions further confirm that these latents are sufficient to recover personalized behavior and that the identified experts are necessary for it. Overall, our proposed method offers principled foundation for understanding and designing more transparent personalized language models.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Personalization of LLMs Methods for aligning LLMs with individual or group preferences (Zhang et al., 2025b) condition on retrieved user history or profile summaries (Salemi et al., 2024; Richardson et al., 2023), encode personas in the prompt (Jiang et al., 2024b), train per-user adapters (Tan et al., 2024), learn personalized reward models or merge preference-specific policies (Cheng et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2024), or steer activations toward users style (Zhang et al., 2025a; Cao et al., 2024). LaMP and LongLaMP (Salemi et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2024) evaluate per-user personalization, while Multifaceted Collection and Bench (Lee et al., 2024) specify group preferences via system messages. These works study dense models as black boxes; we study how sparse MoEs represent personalization. 2 2.2 Mixture-of-Experts LLMs. MoE layers route each token to few experts, decoupling parameter count from compute (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Zoph et al., 2022), and now underlie strong open models such as Mixtral, OLMoE, and Qwen3 (Jiang et al., 2024a; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a). Analyses of routing report specialization at the level of tokens and syntax rather than domains (Jiang et al., 2024a; Xue et al., 2024), semantic routing in controlled settings (Olson et al., 2025), and languagespecific experts identified by contrasting routing frequencies (Bandarkar et al., 2026). Expert-level specialization can be exploited for adaptation and control: Bai et al. (2025) tune routers to identify context-faithful experts, Li et al. (2026) encourage expert divergence during training, and Fayyaz et al. (2026) steer behavior by (de)activating experts. We adopt two-stage router-then-expert adaptation for personalization and relate the resulting routing changes to interpretable persona features. Interpreting model features and fine-tuning. Dense-model neurons are polysemantic (Olah et al., 2020); sparse autoencoders recover more monosemantic features (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024), sparse probing measures how few neurons encode concept (Gurnee et al., 2023), and wider, sparser architectures such as MoEs reduce polysemanticity (Yang et al., 2025b; Herbst et al., 2026). Crosscoders, trained with BatchTopK (Bussmann et al., 2024) and explained automatically (Paulo et al., 2025), isolate latents specific to fine-tuned model and have been applied to chat tuning (Minder et al., 2025) and to MoEdense comparisons (Chaudhari et al., 2026). We diff personalized MoE against its base and map the resulting latents onto the experts that route them.

sections.title: 5 Experimental Settings
sections.content: Data and evaluation. We personalize models and train crosscoders on MULTIFACETED COLLECTION (Lee et al., 2024). Each example pairs user query with system message that encodes group-level preference across four dimensions (style, background knowledge, informativeness, harmlessness), along with preference-aligned response generated by GPT-4-Turbo-0125. We evaluate on three benchmarks: (i) MULTIFACETED BENCH (Lee et al., 2024), which uses the same system-message format but has no preferences in common with the training set; (ii) LaMP (Salemi et al., 2024); and (iii) LongLaMP (Kumar et al., 2024). LaMP and LongLaMP instead require inferring per-user preferences from interaction history. Following Zhang et al. (2025a), we use their user splits and omit the email tasks, whose data is not publicly available. We report METEOR and ROUGE-L against the gold responses. Models and baselines. We study three instruction-tuned MoE LLMs: OLMoE-1B-7B (0125), Qwen3-30B-A3B (2507) and Mixtral-8x7B (v0.1). Each is evaluated without adaptation, after router tuning (RT), and after router and expert tuning (RT+EFT). We compare each MoE model with two dense models, one matching its active and one matching its total parameter count: OLMo-21B/7B, Qwen2.5-3B/32B, and Llama-2-13B/70B for Mixtral, following its technical report  (Table 1)  . The dense baselines are evaluated without adaptation and after PEFT on MULTIFACETED COLLECTION. As reference, we also report JANUS7B and its ORPO/DPO variants (Lee et al., 2024), which are fully parameter-fine-tuned on the MULTIFACETED COLLECTION, indicating the upper bound of performance for LLMs with similar parameter counts. sections.title: 6 Results
sections.content: 6.1 Personalization performance comparison Across model families and evaluation metrics, MoE LLMs outperform dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and for the Qwen and Mixtral families, they match or exceed dense LLMs with similar total parameters (Figure 2). The per-variant results in Table 2 show the same pattern after personalization: personalized MoE LLMs outperform or match personalized dense LLMs with similar active parameters. Router tuning accounts for most of this gain in Qwen3, whereas expert tuning contributes more in Mixtral. Across benchmarks, personalization yields the largest gains on MULTIFACETED BENCH, which shares the training datas (MULTIFACETED COLLECTION) form of preference (group-level preferences given via system messages), and smaller gains on LaMP and LongLaMP, which require transferring to per-user preferences inferred from interaction history. Overall, MoE 5 Figure 4: Ratio ν of scales to explain non-personalized and personalized models via personalized latents and their behavior across dense and MoE LLMs. LLMs achieve competitive personalization while activating only fraction of their parameters, motivating mechanistic analysis of how their experts encode personalization features. 6.2 RQ1: Do Sparse MoE LLMs offer lower polysemanticity, enabling better disentanglement of personalized features? Polysemanticity. To investigate the polysemanticity behavior of neurons in MoE experts compared to dense LLMs, we use k-sparse probing (Gurnee et al., 2023). Following Herbst et al. (2026), we estimate the mean difference of activations between positive and negative tokens per concept and compute the binary classification of probe considering only the top-k neurons with the highest activation difference. For our personalization task, we consider the top 5 most frequent sub-dimensions from MULTIFACETED COLLECTION as concepts for each dimension, resulting in 20 independent concepts. For each concept, we take the response tokens (up to 1024 per response, 100 queries) of samples whose system message specifies that subdimension as positives, and those of samples specifying different sub-dimension of the same dimension as negatives (e.g., formal vs. casual under style), giving about 50,000 tokens per class. Following Herbst et al. (2026), we only consider tokens routed to the target expert for MoE LLMs and identify the best layer containing the expert achieving the highest classification accuracy on the test split (25% split). For dense LLMs, the best layer is that with the highest-performing MLP. Figure 3 illustrates the variance in k-sparse probe classification accuracy from = 64 to = 1 for the MoE and dense LLMs with similar active parameters. MoE LLMs outperform dense LLMs with similar active parameters in the balanced accuracy metric, and the performance gap is wider for the same model family (Olmo, Qwen). The gap remains wide at = 1, verifying monosemantic behavior of MoE experts for personalization. Disentanglement of personalized features. sections.title: 7 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: We presented, to our knowledge, the first mechanistic study of personalization in MoE LLMs. Combining two-stage router-and-expert adaptation for personalization with crosscoder-based interpretability analysis for personalization mechanism shows: (1) MoE LLMs achieve competitive personalization performance than dense LLMs by utilizing only 20% of total parameters. (2) MoE LLMs exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs for personalization and they enable better interpretability of encoded personalization features via crosscoder than dense LLMs. (3) MoE encodes distinct personalization features via different routing paths, enabling better localization and subsequent intervention for controlled personalization.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Models and comparisons. We study three open MoE families and analyze one layer per model, selected by routing divergence. Personalization features may also arise at other layers, and our conclusions may not transfer to other MoE designs (e.g., shared experts or fine-grained expert segmentation). The dense counterparts are matched by active or total parameter count, but differ in pretraining data and recipes, so architectural effects cannot be fully separated from training differences. Data and notion of persona. MultifacetedCollection describes preferences through synthetic system messages over four dimensions, with categorical, long-tailed subdimension labels. This captures group-level preferences rather than individual users, and our experiments are limited to English. Personalization signals in real user histories may be noisier and more entangled than in this controlled setting. Crosscoder fidelity. Crosscoders reconstruct activations imperfectly, and reconstruction quality varies across models (with fractions of variance explained of 0.80 for OLMoE, 0.74 for Qwen330B-A3B, and 0.65 for Mixtral, whose activations have much larger magnitudes and heavier tails). Information in the reconstruction error is invisible to our latent-level analyses, and the set of personalized latents depends on the decoder-norm threshold. BatchTopK training and latent scaling mitigate known sparsity artifacts (Minder et al., 2025), but do not rule them out entirely. Probing. Persona concepts are properties of whole responses, whereas sparse probing labels individual tokens, thereby introducing label noise and lowering absolute scores across all models. Selecting the best of many components favors MoE models, which have more candidates (layers experts); we mitigate this by selecting on test data and reporting test scores, but selection effects may remain, particularly for = 1. Probes measure whether concept is decodable, not whether the model uses it. Expert attribution and causality. Expert sets are derived from routing frequencies at firing tokens and are therefore correlational; they depend on the number of examples, the selection rule, and the background routing rate, and their stability is moderate. Evaluation of generation. ROUGE-L and METEOR measure overlap with reference responses and are imperfect proxies for personalization: response can satisfy preference while diverging from the reference wording, as our steering results illustrate. Sampling-based generation adds variance. Automated explanations rely on an LLM explainer and scorer (Llama-3.3-70BInstruct), whose own biases may shape the descriptions.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Use of AI Assistants. The authors used Claude API to assist with language polishing and grammatical corrections, clarity and coherence. All technical contributions, including experimental design choices and final decisions, were made by the authors.

sections.content: A.1 Crosscoder Crosscoder is an encoder-decoder-based architecture that explains the activations from both finetuned (personalized) and base (non-personalized) LLMs by learning shared dictionary of interpretable concepts (latents). Formally, for the input token xt, let the activations from particular layer of the personalized and non-personalized MoEs be h(l,ft) xt Rd and h(l,base) Rd respectively (d is the model dimension), the encoder of the crosscoder maps those activations to higher dimensional (D >> d)2 latent space, where each dimension {1, . . . , D} explains distinct features encoded in those activations h(l,ft) as: , and h(l,base) xt xt xt the latent h(l,base) xt h(l,ft) xt +e(base) aj(xt) = ReLU(e(ft) +b(enc) ) (10) j, where aj activation for is e(ft) , e(base) Rd are the the encoder weight vectors corresponding to the latent j, and b(enc) is the corresponding encoder bias. The decoder of the crosscoder then reconstructs those activations h(l,ft) for the token xt using the sparse xt activation distribution of shared dictionary latents as: , and h(l,base) xt h(l,ft) xt = h(l,base) xt = (cid:88) (cid:88) aj(xt) d(ft) + b(dec) aj(xt) d(base) + b(dec) (11) where d(ft) Rd are the the decoder weight vectors corresponding to the latent j, and , d(base) 2D = α d, where α is the expansion factor, and we keep it as 32 for our experiments. 11 Figure 11: Layer-wise routing distribution analysis. The crossj coder is trained by minimizing the loss involving (a) reconstruction error as h(l,ft) , and h(l,base) h(l,base) , and (b) sparsity enforcement xt xt on the decoder weights d(ft) , d(base) . Following (Minder et al., 2025) of utilizing L0 sparsity instead of L1 sparsity in obtaining better decoupled latents, we adopt the L0 sparsity-based BatchTopK crosscoder (Bussmann et al., 2024) to select top-k latents activated per example for batch size of n, enforcing only nk activated latents for activation reconstruction from both models. More details about BatchTopk crosscoder are described in Minder et al. (2025).
